title: Prompt engineering that survives contact with production
summary: A prompt that works in a playground often falls apart under real user input. What actually makes prompts reliable at scale: structure, constraints, and treating them like code.

sections.title: 1. The demo prompt vs. the production prompt

blocks.text: A prompt that works beautifully on three hand-picked examples is not a feature — it's a hypothesis. Real users send empty inputs, contradictory instructions, adversarial phrasing, and languages you didn't plan for. The gap between a prompt that demos well and one that holds up in production is almost entirely about handling the inputs you didn't imagine.

The mindset shift is to stop writing prompts as prose and start writing them as specifications: a clear role, explicit constraints, a defined output shape, and stated behavior for edge cases. Vague instructions produce vague, drifting output; precise ones produce results you can build on top of.

sections.title: 2. Structure the output, don't hope for it

blocks.text: If your code has to parse the model's response, don't leave the format to chance. Specify the exact structure and, where the platform supports it, enforce it with a schema. A model asked to 'return some JSON' will occasionally wrap it in prose; a model told exactly which fields to return, and constrained to that shape, is dramatically more reliable.

Return ONLY a JSON object with this exact shape, no prose:
{
  "category": one of ["billing", "technical", "other"],
  "urgency": integer 1-5,
  "summary": one sentence
}
If the input is empty or unintelligible, set category to "other" and urgency to 1.

sections.title: 3. Treat prompts like code you can test

items: Version prompts alongside your codebase, so a change is reviewable and revertable.
Keep a small evaluation set of real, tricky inputs and re-run it whenever the prompt changes.
Always define fallback behavior — what the system does when the model returns something malformed.
Log inputs and outputs so real-world failures become tomorrow's test cases.

blocks.text: The teams who ship reliable AI features aren't the ones with the cleverest prompts. They're the ones who treat prompts as testable, versioned artifacts with defined failure modes — the same discipline they'd apply to any other critical piece of the system.
